params.why: at least one and at most three of the four data sets are categorical, so the count is a real decision and never 0 or 4

stem: A teacher collects four data sets from her class. (a) {=desc[pick[0]]}. (b) {=desc[pick[1]]}. (c) {=desc[pick[2]]}. (d) {=desc[pick[3]]}. How many of these four data sets are qualitative categorical?
solution: For each data set, first decide whether it can be written as numbers. If it cannot, it is qualitative, and then decide whether it is categorical or anecdotal.
Count the data sets that are qualitative categorical: there are {=ans} of them, so the answer is {=ans}.
notes: Advanced tier: several steps. Four data sets are drawn from a fixed bank of twelve (four categorical lists of short answers, four anecdotal sets of three learner sentences, four sets of numbers) and the student must make the book's two-stage decision on each (numbers or not; if not, limited set of possibilities or story) and count the categorical ones. The numeric sets are there so that the first step of the book's solution ('cannot be written as numbers') is exercised; the question never asks discrete versus continuous, which belongs to another objective. The count is restricted to 1 to 3 by a require. Descriptors such as 'each in a sentence of their own' are part of the fixed bank and make the anecdotal sets unambiguous; all data sets are printed with semicolons and no quotes so form is the same across types. The answer is a plain whole number.
